title: A Look at GRIT - JRPG nostalgia on your table
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y8mTWAs2PPw

Daniel (@dungeondive) looks at GRIT, a Game Crafter review copy, and a one- or two-player exploration game that wears its NES and SNES influences openly. It begins with you waking up at home, where, as in so many JRPGs, your mother sends you out to fetch a jug of milk from the farm down the road. From there you reveal a hidden map from a numbered deck of over 200 cards, much as in 7th Continent. QR codes on the cards open a hypertext adventure book online (a PDF version exists for app-averse players).

He shows very little, because he estimates about three-quarters of the game is discovery: of the map, and of what the quest actually is. The structure he does explain is something like Dark Souls. You push out from one checkpoint toward the next on limited health and stamina, and if you die you fall back to your last checkpoint, discarding any items above the number you started with. Skill checks are short web-page choices, such as how to cross a windy bridge. Blacksmiths turn plans plus hide, wood, iron and feathers into equipment.

His main complaint is the eight-page rulebook, which he had to read four times and supplement with the designer's video. The website tracks nothing, so you keep your own quest notes. He'd love a proper app, with chiptunes. At around $50 it's pricey, but "neat" is his word: something like 7th Continent crossed with Quest for the Lost Pixel.

----

GRIT runs its story through QR codes and a website rather than a book or a full app. Where do you draw the line on technology in an exploration game?
